doc.title: Ralph Emerson Brown and Jasper Taylor Interview, 1961-05-23
doc.interviewee: Ralph Emerson Brown and Jasper Taylor

title: Playing Jelly Roll Blues and Junkman Blues in 1916-17
summary: Brown and Taylor recall playing Jelly Roll Blues around 1916-17, when Brown left Hampton, whether it was published, and mix it up with Lucky Roberts's Junkman Blues.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: Well, I first heard of General Roll, through his number, the General Roll Blues. I think he must have written that General Roll Blues. Well, I think he had written that by 16, I believe, in 1960. It seemed like I played it, my first job, job, and I left Hampton, was in the Palastino, north of Virginia. I played trumpet. It looked like we played General Roll Blues. And was it written by that time, General Roll? Or was it?
I don't think it was published, that early. Yeah.
He was in Memphis, La Croix, in Chicago. I was 16, I mean. It seemed like I played General Roll Blues about, long about that time. But I'm not kidding.

Yeah, and he had General Roll Blues. Yeah, I'm not sure. Uh-huh. Yeah, I'm not sure. That's why he came to Hampton to get it, uh, see what he could do with it. So he came to Chicago and rostered it to me.

If I didn't play in 16, I certainly played in 17, because 17 does, yeah, I joined the Oakland Ugly Show, and I know we played it in 17, but it looks like I played in 16. But I know we played in 17. I know well. Quite a hit then, wasn't it? Quite a number.
Nice, nice, nice, nice, nice, nice, nice, nice.
Now that was just an instrumental, it wasn't, no words. I never heard any words.
Yeah. Because later on, maybe somebody did put a word, but I don't remember.
Jelly himself didn't put any words.
No, no he didn't. It was a nice number. Then of course, that number, I used to get that number mixed up with the old Junkman Blues. Lucky Roberts wrote that.
